title: Wuchikittawbut, Montaukett Sunksquaw
summary: Wuchikittawbut, also written Wicchitaubit or Wuch-i-kit-tau-but, was a mid-seventeenth-century Montaukett sunksquaw, widow of Wyandanch, and mother of Wyancombone.
content:
Wuchikittawbut, also written Wicchitaubit or Wuch-i-kit-tau-but, was a mid-seventeenth-century Montaukett sunksquaw, widow of Wyandanch, and mother of Wyancombone. The sources cited here do not establish her birth date and place her death around 1663.

Historical Context

After Wyandanch's death, Wuchikittawbut shared leadership responsibilities connected with her young son, Wyancombone, and is documented in Montaukett land, herbage, beach, and whaling-rights matters.12

Her leadership should be kept distinct from Quashawam, Wyandanch's daughter, who later held the Sunksquaw title in separate records.3

The surviving documents show Native women's authority in diplomacy, land, inheritance, and maritime rights during a period of intense colonial pressure.2

References

  1. Gaynell Stone, The History and Archaeology of the Montauk, index references pp. 690-692.
  2. John A. Strong, America's Early Whalemen: Indian Shore Whalers on Long Island, 1650-1750, p. 41.
  3. John A. Strong, The Montaukett Indians of Eastern Long Island.
why_this_matters: Wuchikittawbut centers Montaukett women's leadership. Her documented leadership shows that Native political authority was not only male and that shoreline, whaling, inheritance, and land rights were central to community survival.
